name: Baba Harbhajan Singh Mandir
tagline: The Army shrine to a soldier who died in 1968
meta_description: Baba Mandir guide: the story of Sepoy Harbhajan Singh, new and old shrines, permits, 2026 cab fares with Tsomgo, altitude tips and visiting etiquette.
summary: Baba Mandir is an Indian Army shrine at about 4,000 m on the road between Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La, about 55 km from Gangtok. It honours Sepoy Harbhajan Singh of the Punjab Regiment, who died near Nathu La in 1968 and is revered by soldiers as a protector. Visit with Tsomgo on one permit.
intro: The shrine most visitors see, often called the new Baba Mandir, stands at a road junction about 18 km beyond Tsomgo Lake, where one road climbs to Nathu La and another runs towards Kupup and the Old Silk Route. It was built by the Army in November 1982 and is run by soldiers posted in the area. The setting is bare, high and windswept, with snow on the slopes for much of the year.

Inside are a portrait and statue of Harbhajan Singh, his uniform, boots and personal belongings, and a small room kept as his quarters. Soldiers and visitors leave offerings and pray for safety. Outside there is a souvenir counter, a tea point and memorial boards that tell his story. The original shrine, his bunker, stands further along the Silk Route side, in what is now Pakyong district.

Baba Mandir is on the same protected-area permit as Tsomgo, and foreigners in groups of two or more can usually visit it, though they cannot go on to Nathu La. At around 4,000 m, keep the visit short and move slowly. It takes 30–45 minutes, usually as part of a 6–9 hour day from Gangtok. Check current status before you travel.

story.title: Sepoy Harbhajan Singh, 1946–1968
story.text: Harbhajan Singh was born into a Sikh family on 30 August 1946 in Sardarpura, in a district that is now in Pakistan. He matriculated from DAV High School in Patti, Punjab, in March 1965, and enlisted at Amritsar in the Punjab Regiment that year. On 4 October 1968, aged 22, he died near Nathu La. According to the board beside his shrine, he fell into a nullah while escorting a mule column from Tuku La to Dongchui La. Soldiers came to believe that he continued to guard the frontier, appearing in dreams to warn of danger, and his story spread through the Army and beyond. In November 1982 the Army built the present shrine at the Kupup road junction. Wikipedia records a long-running custom in which his belongings were sent by train each September to his home village of Kuka in Kapurthala district, accompanied by soldiers, with a berth reserved in his name. He is widely known as 'Baba', and many soldiers posted here still salute his shrine.
story.source: Wikipedia: Baba Harbhajan Singh; memorial board at the shrine

little_known.fact: The present Baba Mandir was built on 11 November 1982 at the junction of the road to Kupup and the trail towards Menmecho Lake; the original shrine is his bunker further along the Silk Route side.
Harbhajan Singh served in the Army for just over three years, from 30 June 1965 until his death on 4 October 1968.
As told locally, visitors leave bottles of water at the shrine and collect them later, believing the water has been blessed; many drivers will offer you one.

facts: Army shrine, soldiers' legend, high mountain road
Tsomgo protected-area permit via registered agent

highlights.title: The shrine and his quarters
highlights.text: The main hall holds Harbhajan Singh's portrait, statue and belongings, and a room is kept as his quarters, with a bed, uniform and boots. Soldiers maintain it with care. Remove your shoes, cover your head if asked and keep your voice low; it is a place of worship.

highlights.title: The memorial boards
highlights.text: Boards outside give his service details and the Army's account of how he died, escorting a mule column from Tuku La to Dongchui La in October 1968. Reading them takes five minutes and explains why soldiers on this frontier still revere him.

highlights.title: The road junction view
highlights.text: The shrine stands where the road splits towards Nathu La and towards Kupup and the Old Silk Route. On clear days you look across high, bare ridges and snowfields, with Kupup's lake country beyond. It is one of the most open views on the whole Tsomgo road.

highlights.title: Tea with the Army
highlights.text: A tea point near the shrine is run for visitors, and a hot drink at around 4,000 m is welcome. Soldiers here are friendly but busy; follow their instructions about parking, photography and time limits.

highlights.title: Open to foreigners
highlights.text: Unlike Nathu La, Baba Mandir is usually covered by the Tsomgo protected-area permit for foreign groups of two or more, so mixed groups can visit together. Foreign members wait here while Indian members continue to Nathu La. Check current status before you travel.

how_to_reach.text: Shared Tsomgo and Baba Mandir tours run daily from Gangtok in season, for about ₹800–1,200 a seat including the shared car. Hand over ID and two photos to the agent the day before. Departures are around 7–8 am, back by mid-afternoon.

A reserved SUV for Tsomgo and Baba Mandir costs about ₹4,500–6,500, or ₹6,500–9,000 with Nathu La. Only Sikkim-registered tourist vehicles on permit can go beyond the check post. The drive from Tsomgo to the shrine is about 18 km, roughly 45 minutes.

Baba Mandir is reached only from Gangtok on a permit day trip, or from the Silk Route side on a Pakyong district Silk Route permit. Spend at least one night in Gangtok first. NH10 from the plains closes in the monsoon; check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: There is no tourist accommodation at Baba Mandir. Stay in Gangtok and visit on the Tsomgo day trip: Hotel Tibet, The Chumbi Residency and Elgin Nor-Khill are convenient for early pickups, while Mintokling Guest House and Hotel Sonam Delek suit budget travellers. Indian travellers doing the Old Silk Route can stay in homestays at Kupup, Gnathang or Zuluk in Pakyong district and visit the old Baba Mandir bunker on the same trip.
tips: Remove shoes, cover your head if asked, and do not photograph inside without permission.
Keep the visit to 30–45 minutes at around 4,000 m and climb the shrine steps slowly.
Carry warm layers and gloves; the junction is exposed and windy in every season.
Foreign members of a group can visit Baba Mandir but must wait here while Indians go to Nathu La.
Follow soldiers' instructions on parking and photography without argument.

experiences.title: Visit the shrine of Baba Harbhajan Singh
experiences.cost: Free; included in Tsomgo circuit car
experiences.summary: Pay respects at the Army-run shrine to Sepoy Harbhajan Singh, who died near Nathu La in 1968 at 22. See his quarters and belongings, read the memorial boards and understand why soldiers on this border still salute him.
body: Park at the junction and walk up to the shrine, built by the Army in November 1982. Shoes come off at the entrance, and you may be asked to cover your head. The main hall holds his portrait and statue surrounded by offerings: flowers, incense, water bottles, small flags. Soldiers keep it immaculate.

A separate room is kept as Harbhajan Singh's quarters, with his bed made, uniform pressed and boots polished. To soldiers this is not a museum but his room. Visitors walk through quietly; some pray, others simply look. Outside, memorial boards give his service record and the Army's account of how he died in October 1968.

Spend no more than 30–45 minutes here at around 4,000 m. Take tea at the visitor point and buy a souvenir if you wish; proceeds support the shrine. Photography inside is usually restricted. Mornings are clearer and calmer. Check current status before you travel, as access depends on road and weather conditions.

faqs.q: Who was Baba Harbhajan Singh?
faqs.a: He was a sepoy of the Punjab Regiment, born in 1946, who died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968, aged 22, after falling into a nullah while escorting a mule column. Soldiers came to believe he still guards the border, and the Army built a shrine to him in 1982.

faqs.q: Is Baba Mandir a Sikh or Hindu temple?
faqs.a: It is best described as an Army shrine. Harbhajan Singh was born into a Sikh family, and soldiers of all faiths visit and pray there. The shrine includes elements of different traditions. Visitors of any background are welcome if they behave respectfully: shoes off, head covered if asked.

faqs.q: Can foreigners visit Baba Mandir?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Baba Mandir is covered by the Tsomgo protected-area permit for foreign groups of two or more, arranged through a registered agent. Foreigners cannot continue to Nathu La, which is for Indian nationals only. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: The old Baba Mandir bunker on the Silk Route
experiences.duration: 1 hour as part of a Silk Route trip
experiences.cost: Included in Silk Route car hire
experiences.image_query: Old Baba Mandir Silk Route Sikkim
experiences.summary: On the Old Silk Route side, beyond the new shrine, stands the original Baba Mandir, built at Harbhajan Singh's bunker. It is reached on Pakyong district's Silk Route circuit, for Indian nationals only, and involves a climb of many steps at high altitude.
body: Before the 1982 shrine was built at the road junction, soldiers honoured Harbhajan Singh at the bunker where he had been posted. That original shrine, now known as the old Baba Mandir, stands further along the high road on the Silk Route side, in what is now Pakyong district. Fewer tourists reach it because of the terrain and the separate permit.

Reaching it involves climbing a long flight of steps at well over 3,500 m. Take it very slowly, with frequent rests, and do not attempt it if you felt unwell at Tsomgo or Nathu La. Inside, the shrine is small and simple, with offerings left by soldiers and pilgrims.

The old Baba Mandir is visited on the Old Silk Route circuit from Rongli or Gangtok, with nights at Zuluk, Gnathang or Kupup. That circuit is for Indian nationals only, with a permit through Rongli. Check current status before you travel. Ask us to combine it with Tsomgo for a two- or three-day high-road trip.

faqs.q: Where is the old Baba Mandir?
faqs.a: The old Baba Mandir stands at Harbhajan Singh's original bunker on the Silk Route side of the high road, beyond the 1982 shrine, in what is now Pakyong district. It is usually visited on Old Silk Route trips with nights at Zuluk, Gnathang or Kupup, not on the standard Tsomgo day trip.

faqs.q: Is the old Baba Mandir difficult to reach?
faqs.a: It involves climbing many steps at high altitude, above 3,500 m, which is hard work even for fit people. Go slowly and rest often. Skip it if anyone in your group has heart or lung problems or felt unwell earlier in the trip. Younger children should be carried or stay below.

faqs.q: Can we visit the old and new Baba Mandir on the same day?
faqs.a: Only on an itinerary that combines the Tsomgo road with the Old Silk Route, which needs the right permits and is for Indian nationals only. We usually plan it as a two- or three-day trip with a night at Gnathang or Zuluk. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Photographing the high road to Baba Mandir
experiences.image_query: road Tsomgo to Baba Mandir snow Sikkim
experiences.summary: The 18 km from Tsomgo to Baba Mandir climbs through some of the most open country on the Gangtok road: switchbacks, snowfields, yak pastures and long ridgelines. How to get good pictures while respecting military rules.
body: Beyond Tsomgo the forest thins out and the road climbs over open slopes towards the junction at about 4,000 m. In April and May, snow walls line parts of the road; in October and November the grass turns gold and the sky is often clear. Yaks graze near herders' huts in summer.

This is a militarised area. Never photograph Army camps, vehicles, soldiers, bridges or installations, and never fly a drone. Ask your driver where stopping is allowed: many bends are narrow and stopping blocks convoys. Safe pull-outs near the junction and near Tsomgo are the usual places for photographs.

Light is best in the first hours of the morning, before cloud builds. Use a polariser for the deep blue sky, and keep batteries warm in an inside pocket, as they drain quickly in the cold. Above all, do not let photography stretch your time at altitude: keep moving slowly and keep to schedule.

faqs.q: Can we use a drone near Baba Mandir or Tsomgo?
faqs.a: No. The Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La area is a militarised border zone, and drones are strictly prohibited without special government permission, which tourists do not get. Flying one can lead to confiscation and legal trouble. Use a phone or camera from permitted spots only.

faqs.q: Where can we stop for photographs on the Baba Mandir road?
faqs.a: Stop only where your driver says it is safe and allowed, usually at wider pull-outs near Tsomgo and near the Baba Mandir junction. Many bends are narrow, and stopping can block Army convoys. Never photograph military camps, vehicles or soldiers.

faqs.q: When is the best light for photographs on the Tsomgo road?
faqs.a: Early morning, roughly 7–10 am, usually gives the clearest skies and softest light. Cloud often builds by noon, especially from May to September. October and November are the most reliable months; April and May are best for snow and some flowers lower down.

experiences.title: A gentle high-road day for seniors
experiences.summary: How we plan Tsomgo and Baba Mandir for older travellers and anyone worried about altitude: a later start, more stops, short visits at the top and a quiet afternoon. Simple steps that make the high road comfortable for most healthy people.
body: Going from Gangtok's 1,650 m to about 4,000 m in three hours is a big jump. For older travellers we always plan at least two nights in Gangtok first, then a reserved car rather than a shared jeep, so we control the pace. We start around 8 am instead of 7, after a light breakfast, with water and simple snacks in the car.

On the way up we stop at Kyongnosla for a short break, then go straight to Baba Mandir and keep the visit there to about 30 minutes, helping with the shrine steps. On the way down we stop at Tsomgo, which is lower, for tea and a short lakeside walk, before heading back to Gangtok.

Anyone with heart disease, high blood pressure, lung problems or recent surgery should consult a doctor before the trip. Carry regular medicines and a warm layer. Watch for severe headache, breathlessness at rest or confusion, and descend at once if they appear. We skip Nathu La for seniors unless they feel strong.

faqs.q: Is Baba Mandir safe for elderly travellers?
faqs.a: Many healthy seniors visit without problems, but about 4,000 m is high. Spend two nights in Gangtok first, keep the visit short, climb the steps slowly and avoid exertion. Anyone with heart or lung disease should consult a doctor first. We plan gentler days for older guests on request.

faqs.q: Should we carry oxygen to Tsomgo and Baba Mandir?
faqs.a: Small canned oxygen is sold in Gangtok and some drivers carry it, but it gives only brief relief and is not a treatment. The real remedy for altitude sickness is going down. Acclimatise in Gangtok, go slowly and keep visits short. Consult a doctor if you have health concerns.

faqs.q: What are the signs of altitude sickness?
faqs.a: Common early signs are headache, nausea, dizziness, tiredness and poor sleep. Danger signs are severe headache, vomiting, breathlessness at rest, confusion or unsteady walking. If these appear, descend immediately and seek medical help. On a Tsomgo day trip, simply driving down usually brings quick relief.

faqs.q: Where is Baba Mandir in Sikkim?
faqs.a: The new Baba Mandir is about 55 km from Gangtok, roughly 18 km beyond Tsomgo Lake, at the junction where roads go to Nathu La and to Kupup. It stands at about 4,000 m. The original shrine, the old Baba Mandir, is further along the Silk Route side in Pakyong district.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit for Baba Mandir?
faqs.a: Yes. Baba Mandir is inside the protected area covered by the Tsomgo permit, arranged through a registered agent a day ahead with ID and photos. Indians and foreign groups of two or more can visit. Check current status before you travel, as rules change.

faqs.q: How much time is needed at Baba Mandir?
faqs.a: About 30–45 minutes is enough to visit the shrine, see his quarters, read the memorial boards and have tea. Longer is not advisable at around 4,000 m. The whole Tsomgo and Baba Mandir trip takes 6–7 hours return from Gangtok.

faqs.q: Is Baba Mandir open every day?
faqs.a: It is usually open daily for visitors on the Tsomgo permit, though access depends on road conditions, snow and security. Nathu La, beyond it, is usually closed on Mondays and Tuesdays. Check current status before you travel, and keep a spare day in Gangtok.

faqs.q: What is the story of Baba Harbhajan Singh?
faqs.a: He was a 22-year-old sepoy of the Punjab Regiment who died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968, falling into a nullah while escorting a mule column. Soldiers came to believe he still protects the frontier, and the Army built his shrine in 1982.

faqs.q: Can we visit Baba Mandir without going to Nathu La?
faqs.a: Yes. The standard Tsomgo and Baba Mandir trip does not include Nathu La, and it is the usual plan for foreigners, families with small children and anyone travelling on Mondays or Tuesdays. A reserved car costs about ₹4,500–6,500 for this shorter circuit.

faqs.q: What should we wear to Baba Mandir?
faqs.a: Dress warmly in layers: thermal, fleece and a windproof or padded jacket, with gloves and a hat. Wear shoes that slip off easily, as you remove them at the shrine. Women may be asked to cover their heads; carry a scarf. Sunglasses help against snow glare.

faqs.q: Is there food at Baba Mandir?
faqs.a: There is a tea point and usually simple snacks near the shrine. For a proper meal, eat at the Tsomgo stalls or wait until you return to Gangtok. Carry water and snacks in the car, especially for children, as the day is long and food options are limited.

faqs.q: Why do people leave water bottles at Baba Mandir?
faqs.a: As told locally, visitors leave bottles of water at the shrine and collect them later, believing the water is blessed. Many drivers and soldiers will explain the custom. Take your bottle back with you; do not leave plastic behind in the mountains.
